Clark's growth curve reserves

Source: R/reserving_extras.R
clark_growth.Rd

Reserves from a growth curve fitted to the incremental claims by maximum likelihood, after Clark (2003): the LDF method, with an ultimate for each origin, or the Cape Cod method, with one expected loss ratio on the premiums. Its standard errors have a process part and a parameter part.

Usage

clark_growth(
  triangle,
  curve = c("loglogistic", "weibull"),
  premium = NULL,
  method = c("ldf", "cape cod"),
  truncation = Inf,
  offset = 0.5
)

Arguments

triangle

A triangle of cumulative claims, as for chain_ladder.

curve

"loglogistic" (the default) or "weibull".

premium

The premium of each origin: needed by the Cape Cod method, and used for the loss ratios when given to the LDF method.

method

"ldf" (the default) or "cape cod".

truncation

The age, in development periods, at which the curve is cut off and the claims are taken to be fully developed: Inf (the default) for none.

offset

The average date of the claims in an origin period, as a share of a period from its start: 0.5 (the default) for claims spread evenly over it, 0 to measure ages from the start.

Value

An object of class netsimr_reserve: a list with by_origin, a data frame with each origin's latest claims, share developed, ultimate, IBNR, standard error, coefficient of variation and its process and parameter parts (and premium and ultimate loss ratio when there are premiums); total; parameters, the curve's \(\omega\) and \(\theta\) (and the loss ratio of the Cape Cod method), \(\sigma^2\) and the degrees of freedom; growth, the fitted curve as a function of the age; fitted and residuals, the fitted increments and the Pearson residuals \((c - \mu) / \sqrt{\sigma^2 \mu}\), as triangles; and covariance.

Details

The share of an origin's ultimate developed by age \(x\) is a growth curve: the log-logistic \(G(x) = x^\omega / (x^\omega + \theta^\omega)\) or the Weibull \(G(x) = 1 - e^{-(x / \theta)^\omega}\). The age is measured from the average date of the claims in an origin period, offset of a period after its start (a half for claims spread evenly over it), so the increment of development period \(t\) is expected to be \(\mu_{it} = U_i (G(t - o) - G(t - 1 - o))\), with \(G = 0\) at ages up to 0. \(U_i\) is the ultimate of each origin (LDF method) or its premium times one expected loss ratio (Cape Cod method). The increments are taken to be over-dispersed Poisson: the parameters maximise \(\sum c_{it} \log \mu_{it} - \mu_{it}\), so that each \(U_i\) (or the loss ratio) has a closed form given \(\omega\) and \(\theta\), which are found numerically. The scale \(\sigma^2\) is the sum of the squared Pearson residuals over the degrees of freedom (the cells less the parameters).

The reserve of an origin is \(U_i (G(T - o) - G(a_i - o))\), from its latest age \(a_i\) to the truncation age \(T\) (infinite by default; the growth curves can have long tails, so a finite truncation is often used with the LDF method). Its process variance is \(\sigma^2\) times the reserve; its parameter variance comes from the covariance of the parameters, \(\sigma^2\) times the inverse of minus the second derivatives of the log-likelihood, by the delta method. The results agree with the ChainLadder package's ClarkLDF() and ClarkCapeCod().

References

Clark, D. R. (2003). LDF curve-fitting and stochastic reserving: a maximum likelihood approach. Casualty Actuarial Society Forum, Fall 2003, 41-92.

See also

chain_ladder and cape_cod.
